canberra.title: ACTU picks 38-year-old campaigner as its next president
canberra.snippet: Career unionist Emma Kingdon will become the next president of the Australian Council of Trade Unions, taking over from Michele O’Neil in...
canberra.content:
New ACTU President Emma Kingdon (centre) will start her new role in December. Photo: ACTU.

Career unionist Emma Kingdon will become the next president of the Australian Council of Trade Unions, taking over from Michele O’Neil in December.

The ACTU Executive met on Tuesday (20 October) and named Ms Kingdon as the president-elect of the peak union body.

Her appointment completes the ACTU’s transition to a new leadership team, following the resignations of Ms O’Neil, who steps down in December, and former secretary Sally McManus, who left in August and was replaced by new secretary Melissa Donnelly.

For the past nine months, Ms Kingdon, 38, has worked as the executive officer of the CFMEU Administration, which is tasked with rebuilding the disgraced union.

She previously worked at the ACTU for 10 years in several roles, including on the leadership team as its national campaigns director.

In that role, she drove record growth in union membership.

Ms Donnelly welcomed the appointment of a new president to work with her at the helm of the ACTU.

“Emma Kingdon has been a grassroots union organiser representing workers in early childhood education and aged care to win higher wages in these low-paid sectors,” she said.

“Emma also dealt with some of the toughest corporate bosses in the major banks and has never left a negotiating table or a picket line without getting the best possible outcomes for her members.

“Emma is a highly experienced campaigner who led union campaigns that have protected and advanced workers’ rights, helped to overturn bad workplace laws and helped to boost union membership.

“She has also taken on hard challenges, including her work in the CFMEU Administration, which is tasked with rebuilding the union free of the corruption and criminality that has taken hold in the construction industry.”

Ms Kingdon is a former union organiser and campaign director, who grew up in a working-class family in Perth’s outer-suburban Rockingham.

She started in a fast-food outlet, where she joined the retail workers’ union, the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees’ Association (SDA), before becoming a union organiser with the United Workers Union (UWU) and the Finance Sector Union (FSU).

At the UWU in Western Australia and New South Wales, Ms Kingdon organised lower-paid workers, mainly women, in sectors such as early childhood education and care and aged care.

At the FSU, she worked with finance workers to build collective strength to take on some of Australia’s largest corporations.

She pushed for fairer treatment of workers made redundant at NAB, saving jobs and livelihoods and led a successful campaign against Westpac Banking Corporation’s plan to offshore local jobs from a regional call centre.

Ms Kingdon said she grew up in a working-class family and “gets” how hard it is to make ends meet.

“And that is what drives me every day to see workers get ahead,” she said.

“What I’ve learnt is the power to change things comes from us – working people sticking together.

“It is what has made our country great, when we put aside our differences and support each other, we win great things like Medicare, wage rises and our rights at work.

“Too many workers are having to look at their budgets and wondering what else they can cut because the system feels rigged when your pay can’t keep up with the cost of living.”

Ms O’Neil congratulated Ms Kingdon on her appointment as president-elect, describing her as a “highly effective and formidable” union campaigner.

“Her deep understanding of the issues facing workers today, commitment to fairness and strategic mindset will be an asset for workers and their unions that have backed her to become the next president of the ACTU,” the outgoing president said.

“I am confident that I am leaving the role of president in very good hands. The leadership team of Emma Kingdon and Melissa Donnelly represent a new generation of strong, smart, effective representatives of working people.

“Emma expects workers to be able to turn up to work and be treated with dignity and respect, get paid fairly and have safe and good working conditions.

“Working Australians should know they have a strong and determined advocate to fight in their corner.”

canberra.title: Extra Anzac Day public holiday proposed, but businesses warn of $35 million hit
canberra.snippet: The ACT Government has moved to guarantee an Anzac Day public holiday every year, including an extra day off when it falls on a weekend, ...
canberra.content:
The ACT Government has introduced legislation to guarantee an Anzac Day public holiday every year, with an additional day off when it falls on a weekend. Photo: Australian War Memorial.

The ACT Government has moved to guarantee an Anzac Day public holiday every year, including an extra day off when it falls on a weekend, but Canberra’s peak business body warns the change could cost businesses up to $35 million in lost productivity.

The Canberra Business Chamber says the proposal would add to already rising costs for small businesses, while the government argues it will protect workers’ entitlements and give employers greater certainty.

Under legislation introduced in the ACT Legislative Assembly on Wednesday (21 October), 25 April would remain a public holiday regardless of which day of the week it falls on. And should Anzac Day fall on a Saturday or Sunday, the following Monday would also be a public holiday.

Canberra Business Chamber chief executive Greg Harford said the Chamber fully supported recognising Anzac Day but opposed the additional Monday holiday.

“The Canberra Business Chamber completely endorses a public holiday every year on 25 April, as a mark of respect for those who have served, fought and died for Australia,” he said.

However, he said the government had failed to understand the financial pressure the extra holiday would place on businesses.

“This decision is deeply disappointing and demonstrates that the government has not understood the costs and impacts on the private sector and on small business,” Mr Harford said.

The Chamber estimates the proposal would reduce productivity by between $30 million and $35 million a year and increase direct wage costs for businesses that remain open by between 125 and 200 per cent. Mr Harford said small business owners would either have to pay employees for an additional day off or meet higher penalty rates to keep operating.

He also questioned whether the government had properly assessed the financial impact before introducing the legislation.

“The decision makes no economic sense, and the Chamber is concerned that there appears to have been no proper cost-benefit analysis of the proposal undertaken,” he said.

The Chamber warned that the changes would put ACT businesses at a disadvantage compared with those in other jurisdictions.

Introducing the Holidays (Anzac Day) Amendment Bill 2026, Skills, Training and Industrial Relations Minister Michael Pettersson acknowledged that consultation with businesses, unions, veterans’ representatives and other stakeholders had produced mixed views.

But he argued that Anzac Day deserved the same public holiday treatment as Boxing Day.

“I have considered them carefully, but ultimately it’s untenable in my mind that Anzac Day would have a lesser treatment than Boxing Day,” he told the Assembly.

Mr Pettersson said the government wanted to settle the issue now rather than continue making separate public holiday declarations whenever Anzac Day falls on a weekend.

“While I appreciate it is not every day that this assembly debates matters so far in advance, in the interest of providing certainty to employers and employees alike, I think it is important to settle this matter now,” he said.

Under the current arrangements, the government considers additional Anzac Day public holidays on a case-by-case basis. Extra public holidays were declared in 2020, 2021 and 2026.

The minister said permanent arrangements would give workers a guaranteed day off while allowing businesses to plan ahead.

He said Anzac Day was a significant occasion for veterans, their families and the wider community, and the legislation would ensure people had the opportunity to observe it.

The proposal follows public consultation held between 14 August and 11 September. While stakeholders agreed on the importance of Anzac Day, they were divided over whether an additional public holiday was necessary.

Mr Harford said the Chamber provided detailed feedback during the consultation but believed its concerns were ignored.

“We should be looking after ACT businesses, not piling extra costs on them during a cost of doing business crisis,” he said.

Anzac Day will not fall on a weekend again until 2032. Over the next 15 years, it will fall on a weekend four times. Debate on the Bill has been adjourned to a later sitting of the Assembly.

canberra.title: Sex claims, personal attacks and no admins? Canberra Facebook group descends into chaos
canberra.snippet: A Facebook group with more than 10,000 members in Canberra has come under fire after a weekend of sexually suggestive posts, bizarre preg...
canberra.content:
Over sexually suggestive posts, personal allegations and concerns about a lack of moderation have been raised about the Canberra Community Group. Photo: John Lomnicki.

A Facebook group with more than 10,000 members in Canberra has come under fire after a weekend of sexually suggestive posts, bizarre pregnancy claims and personal allegations involving named individuals, leaving members questioning whether the community platform has become a free-for-all.

The Canberra Community Facebook group, intended as a space for residents to exchange information and discuss local issues, has instead become the centre of a heated debate about offensive content, online accountability and the apparent absence of administrators.

Over the weekend, posts ranged from sexual propositions to claims involving identifiable people. Some drew laughing emojis and sarcastic responses, while others prompted members to ask why the group was allowing such content. The names of those targeted are being withheld.

Group member Jonathan Mutton was among those raising concerns, calling for more responsible discussions while acknowledging that administrators could not reasonably be expected to monitor the group around the clock.

“What is going on with this Facebook group at the moment?” he asked.

“There have been sexual posts, personal accusations and serious allegations naming people, with some comments turning it all into a joke.”

“I enjoy a laugh, but serious allegations need to be treated carefully, and people deserve respect.”

Mr Mutton called for clearer rules and more consistent moderation, questioning whether administrators were reviewing the posts and comments. His intervention drew mixed reactions.

One commenter challenged him to volunteer for 24-hour administration, while another claimed the group listed no administrators.

“Admins are meant to monitor 24/7. There are no actual admins listed for the group,” the commenter wrote.

Another member tagged Facebook-related accounts and called for the group to be cleaned up. Others dismissed the controversy with sarcasm.

“Lol this group has really gone to shit,” one member simply wrote.

Another described it as a joke of a Facebook group, prompting the reply, “Yet here you are.”

The exchanges exposed a divide between members who appeared to treat the posts as entertainment and those concerned about the reputational harm that unverified accusations could cause.

Region also could not find any details about the administrators or a way to connect to the page. The objectionable posts were also neither reported nor removed after being up for over 48 hours. A day later, the group was business as usual, with people posting business ads.

The controversy comes just weeks after another Canberra Facebook group adopted a tougher approach to online behaviour.

In September, Canberra Notice Board Group announced it would expose members’ profiles using nicknames to make abusive, inflammatory or potentially defamatory comments.

From 2 September, administrators warned that members breaching the rules could have screenshots of their personal Facebook profiles published alongside the offending content. Repeat offenders also risked permanent bans.

“Unfortunately, we have seen an increasing number of members using Facebook’s nickname feature to make comments or posts they may not otherwise make under their own name.

“Using a nickname does not remove your responsibility for what you post.”

The decision sparked debate about privacy and accountability, particularly whether publicly identifying users was an appropriate response to online abuse.

But offensive posts can also carry legal consequences.

In an earlier interview with Region about social media defamation, BDN Lawyers solicitor Allara Freedman warned that legal action could be costly, complicated and prolonged.

“Suing someone is not only shockingly expensive, but the process can take years,” Ms Freedman said.

She pointed to the landmark 2021 High Court decision involving former Northern Territory youth detainee Dylan Voller, who pursued defamation proceedings against media organisations over third-party comments on their Facebook pages.

The High Court found that the organisations were publishers of those comments because they had facilitated their publication, although the decision did not itself determine whether the comments were defamatory.

“Put simply, if the commenting wasn’t made possible by the page itself, the defamation wouldn’t have occurred,” Ms Freedman explained in the earlier interview.

Her comments concerned social media defamation generally, not the current Canberra Community controversy. Whether a particular post or group administrator faces legal liability depends on the circumstances and applicable law.

Meanwhile, Mr Mutton said he was considering leaving the group if the situation continued. “Can we get back to useful Canberra updates and respectful discussions?”

canberra.title: Weekend Northbourne Avenue light rail construction closures cancelled
canberra.snippet: Northbourne Avenue traffic will be slightly less complicated this weekend, with previously announced road closures now cancelled. Infrast...
canberra.content:
21 October 2026

Start the conversation

Some light rail stage 2A construction works have been completed ahead of schedule, removing the need for a weekend closure of Northbourne Avenue. Photo: ACT Government.

Northbourne Avenue traffic will be slightly less complicated this weekend, with previously announced road closures now cancelled.

Infrastructure Canberra said the closures from 8 pm Friday, 23 October, to 6 am Monday, 26 October, for light rail stage 2A works no longer need to go ahead.

“The closures were required to allow for asphalting, traffic barrier setup and removal, and the clean-up and reinstatement of the site,” it read.

“A partial closure of Northbourne Avenue planned from 1 am to 5 am, Sunday, 1 November, will also no longer be required.

“All the necessary works were completed during last weekend’s closure of Northbourne Avenue, and accordingly no further closures are required this weekend.”

Essential works on rail, signalling, communications, utilities and supporting landscaping will still take place around the light rail Alinga Street stop, Northbourne Avenue and the Rudd Street/Bunda Street intersection over the weekend of 31 October and 1 November.

This means the planned replacement buses for the entire light rail network will still run from the first service on Saturday to the last service on Sunday.

“Rail replacement buses, operated by CDC Canberra, will operate in both directions and service every stop along the light rail corridor,” the Infrastructure Canberra statement read.

“These services will run at approximately the same or better frequency of timetabled light rail services.”

Works are also continuing on Commonwealth Avenue. This means Commonwealth Avenue northbound is temporarily reduced to one lane between Albert Street and Vernon Circle.

People have been encouraged to allow extra travel time and to check Transport Canberra for information on rail replacement bus stop locations and service details.

canberra.title: ‘Fed up’ public school teachers take to the streets as threat of Term 4 full-day strike looms
canberra.snippet: Teachers could see a new pay and conditions offer land on their desks in the next few weeks, but union members have warned it better be g...
canberra.content:
A new pay and conditions offer for public school teachers is expected to go to a ballot in the coming weeks. Photo: John Lomnicki.

Teachers could see a new pay and conditions offer land on their desks in the next few weeks, but union members have warned it better be good or Term 4 will see another full-day strike.

Australian Education Union ACT members gathered at Dickson Library and on Northbourne Avenue – as well as outside their schools – this morning (21 October) as part of week-long rolling stop-work action.

College teacher Andrew Hirschfeld is in his second year of teaching. He’d heard the narrative of teachers burning out under increasing workloads and pressure, but experiencing it was entirely different.

“It’s non-stop,” he said.

“When it’s one of those things you live every day, it’s hard to break down into words.”

Mr Hirschfeld described the pressure of not taking time off work for illness, because teachers knew there wouldn’t be enough cover, resulting in their classes being ‘flexed ‘.

He also talked about frustrations that teacher concerns weren’t being listened to – either by the Education Directorate or the ACT Board of Senior Secondary Studies (BSSS).

“A lot of problems dealt with every day [at a college level] are with the BSSS,” Mr Hirschfeld said.

“They’re the ones asking us to store tests for years on end, to scan everything into the system.”

He gave his own workplace, Narrabundah College, as an example of where he felt a “disconnect” between what teachers wanted and what the Education Directorate thought they wanted.

Three buildings at the college were knocked down in 2016 and were replaced with demountables.

Construction on a permanent structure as part of the Narrabundah College Modernisation project is underway, but Mr Hirschfeld said it wouldn’t be fit for purpose for the school’s operations.

The building will contain two Hospitality/Vocational Education Training and Food Technology kitchens, despite only 20 students generally choosing to study food tech.

“So that’s two classrooms that are not at all needed,” Mr Hirschfeld said.

“But the [building’s] ceramics room can only fit 12 students, despite it being a very popular class – they all won’t fit inside.

“It’s that classic situation where we call out for the things we need, but we’re not listened to at all.”

High school teacher Lauren Bingley has worked for almost 10 years and said the industrial action was a clear indication that “things have gotten pretty dire” in recent years.

She’s seen teachers take on more and more administrative and communication responsibilities without the resources to do them properly.

“It’s definitely a lot more difficult being a teacher now; there are a lot more roles and responsibilities put on us that would be okay to cover if we had the resources to do more,” she explained.

“But it seems never-ending to do all those roles, before even getting to lesson planning and teaching.”

Ms Bingley especially struggles with having to combine or flex classes, as she’s seen how it affects students’ ambition to learn.

“When you’ve got 100 kids in the library with two teachers basically babysitting, not a lot of teaching is happening,” she said.

“If kids have that multiple times a day or week … there’s definitely a loss of motivation, and a rise in them feeling disconnected from their learning.

“When it happens too often, that’s a really significant chunk of learning that they’ve missed … and it’s hard to get them re-engaged.”

Union members took to the streets as part of rolling stop-work actions to secure teachers better pay and conditions. Photo: John Lomnicki.

Both union representatives felt the Education Directorate and ACT Government were stringing educators and teachers along during this latest enterprise bargaining round.

Mr Hirschfeld questioned why they didn’t receive their first offer until six months after the last agreement had ended.

“We well and truly should have been striking since the very start,” he said.

“Teachers are fed up.”

Ms Bingley said the next deal needed to show serious improvement, not just better pay and conditions for teachers, but also to show the community that their profession was valued.

“We need the resources to run our schools and to give students the learning that they deserve, plus have functional workplaces for our teachers,” she said.

“When we don’t have the resources and teachers, it all falls apart.”

Education Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith told the Legislative Assembly during question time that the government was working to resolve the enterprise bargaining quickly.

A full-day workshop was held with AEU ACT representatives last week to talk about the staffing guarantee claim, and another meeting was held to work through every single clause and claims drafting.

“I believe that the union has been clear that bargaining is now progressing well,” Ms Rachel Stephen-Smith said.

“We are really hoping to get a further offer to the union … in the next couple of weeks so we can get the agreement out to ballot.”

But without a better deal, the foreshadowed Term 4 full-day strikes seem increasingly likely.

“I think most people will be looking at [the latest deal when it arrives] and thinking: am I going to be able to live with this for the next three years?” Mr Hirschfeld said.

“The majority of teachers understand that striking is what we need to be doing right now – we need to be fighting.”

australia.title: Helen Haines has lost her legs after an alleged attack. Here’s what we know so far
australia.snippet: Independent MP for Victorian seat of Indi in stable condition after incident on Monday afternoon Follow our live blog for latest updates ...
australia.content:
Helen Haines, the independent federal MP for the Victorian seat of Indi, has had both legs amputated but is in a stable condition after an alleged attack in Wangaratta on Monday afternoon.

The incident happened about 3.35pm and involved a four-wheel drive outside Haines’ electorate office. The 65-year-old underwent surgery at Melbourne’s Alfred hospital and is in a critical but stable condition.

australia.title: Soft-spoken David Pocock has big ambitions – but first he wants politicians to ‘double down’ on kindness
australia.snippet: Independent senator’s goals ‘much bigger’ than prime ministership, he reveals in first speech to National Press Club Get our new politica...
australia.content:
He’s six foot tall and full of muscle, but David Pocock’s real strength is often sounding like the most sensible, commonsense voice in the room.

At his first speech to the National Press Club on Wednesday, he said he wasn’t launching a bid for prime minister – no matter how much some people might like the softly spoken senator to have more say in federal politics.

Indeed, Pocock said he was already thinking about life after politics, admitting “you can’t do this for ever”. But before the full-time whistle on his parliamentary career, the former rugby star has a match against his toughest opponent yet: the two-party system.

“I want to be part of building a political system that actually delivers for Australians, no matter who is prime minister,” the ACT senator said.

“I see an opportunity at the next election for a new kind of community political collective … I want to use what I’ve learned over the past four-and-a-half years to help.”

He called for a higher calibre of politics after the alleged attack on the independent Indi MP, Helen Haines. He branded parliament’s question time a “disgrace”, urging a “better standard” among colleagues “to take some of the edge off it”.

Speaking directly about Haines, he said parliament must “meet this [alleged] attack on you by doubling down on the values you represent” – listing transparency, accountability and kindness.

In front of staff and allies – including the ACT politician Thomas Emerson, Pocock’s former staffer and lookalike, as well as the Cheek Media founder and Grayndler independent candidate, Hannah Ferguson – he called for three key policy reforms:

  • A 25% tax on gas exports, which he said could fund anything from boosting welfare to health reforms and aged care.

  • A 5% levy on datacentres to capture more benefits from the AI boom.

  • Transparency reforms to shine a light on lobbyists, secret meetings with politicians and vested interests.

Just two months of gas tax revenue would pay for 100,000 home support packages, while prosthetic eyes and noses for cancer victims would be paid for in three hours, he said. Pocock recounted the moment a woman sat sobbing in his office, so destitute on the miserable jobseeker allowance that she ate dog food because she hadn’t eaten meat in so long.

“A 25% gas export tax could help change that, allowing us to have a social security system that keeps people above the poverty line,” he said.

All politicians have these stories, even if not all of them talk about them with such emotion. Politics is a series of choices and priorities and, presented by Pocock in this way, the choice not to fund welfare boosts or aged care or cancer care is hard to justify.

Asked later about calls for budget discipline and cutting spending, Pocock replied instantly: “You can make cuts, or you can grow revenue.”

“I don’t understand why we’re slugging everyday Aussies and yet we’re happy to export gas for free.”

Despite having only one vote in parliament, and no longer holding the Senate balance of power, Pocock has been extraordinarily successful in drawing attention to his key issues. Labor members are not his biggest fans, but he has moulded the gas tax narrative to the point that government MPs’ social media feeds are flooded with comments demanding change.

Bending the national conversation around a complicated resources tax, to the point where the actual prime minister has to wade through swathes of comments from political normies on every post, shows some level of leadership. Not that Pocock is angling to win that position himself; for one, he said he’s staying in the Senate, not switching to the lower house.

For another, when he told the audience “don’t get ahead of yourselves with ‘Pocock launches bid for PM’ headlines”, it got only the second-biggest laugh in the room.

The biggest laugh came when he added: “My ambition is much bigger than that.”

His idea for a new “coalition” of independents was light on detail, but he said he wanted to “build” something alongside communities which were already organising. Pocock suggested an alliance of independents and collectives like the Community Strong movement headlined by Zali Steggall and Allegra Spender, going on to shout out independent tilts in the ACT electorates of Bean, Canberra and Fenner, where his local campaign infrastructure could make a difference, but also the seat of Fisher and even Anthony Albanese’s, Grayndler.

The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, has said he wants his party to replace Labor. A Pocock-backed independent in Ferguson, replacing the prime minister in his own seat, would be a whole new level.

“I believe a model of smaller, community interest parties and independents working together in an alliance can succeed here and build the kind of future we want,” Pocock said.

Where that ends up, and if it gets off the ground, will be seen in coming months and years. Just don’t expect to see Pocock – rugby star, conservationist, senator, father – add prime minister to his CV anytime soon.

australia.title: Brendan Nugent stares in silence as a court hears about his alleged attack on Helen Haines
australia.snippet: There were no family or friends inside the Wangaratta magistrates court to support the accused, a 43-year-old from Tarrawingee Follow our...
australia.content:
The media pack was so large when it descended on Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday morning that not everyone could fit in the courtroom. They spilled into the hallway, forced to try to log in remotely or pick up clues from afar.

Everyone was hoping to catch a glimpse of Brendan Nugent, who was arrested less than 100 metres away two days earlier after allegedly ramming the independent MP Helen Haines twice in a targeted attack outside her electorate office.

That office remained shuttered on Wednesday and eerily quiet, but for dozens of flowers and cards that had been left for Haines. The MP has had both legs amputated but is in a stable condition in hospital.

The 43-year-old’s motive remains under investigation, and a mystery to the dozens of reporters crammed into courtroom two. He said nothing during his brief hearing, and stared straight ahead, looking downcast in a grey jumper, with a long beard.

He did not request bail, and will remain in custody until a committal mention on 4 February next year.

The magistrate, Allison Vaughan, noted Nugent had mental health and neurological concerns, and that it was his first time in custody.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

His lawyer, Chirag Patel, said Nugent suffered from idiopathic transverse myelitis – a rare neurological condition caused by inflammation of the spinal cord, which can result in muscle weakness, pain and bladder dysfunction. He was also concussed, Patel said.

He is not on any prescribed medication and Patel said he was not withdrawing from any substances, however Vaughan asked a mental health professional to see Nugent immediately after he appeared in court.

It was his first time in custody – and one of the most significant media cases in what typically operates as a quiet regional courthouse.

Bemused onlookers stood on the sidelines.

There were no family or friends there to support Nugent in court. The only local resident was a neighbour from Tarrawingee who sat, resolute, in the front row.

The neighbour, who asked for their name to be withheld, said they were shaking but “wanted to look him in the eye”.

“I felt it was something I needed to do,” the neighbour told Guardian Australia after court. “I didn’t know if I was doing the right thing, but I’m really glad I have now. It’s like it’s finishing off a very bad chapter in our life.”

In a matter of minutes, the hearing was over, and Nugent exited through the back door. Cameras swarmed at the rear exit, positioning their lenses through a fence. Others waited on the top of a nearby car park, hoping to snap a shot from afar.

As Nugent returns to a prison cell, the community continues to rally around their local member. Haines is a beloved MP, highly active in her community, not only during her time in parliament but also throughout her extensive career in healthcare.

She was a midwife to many locals. Nugent’s father revealed on Tuesday they’d been friends for decades. This hits close.

With the media pack remaining centred on the courthouse, the flowers, balloons and notes of appreciation continued to grow at Haines’ nearby electorate office, many in the signature orange of the regional independent movement.

“To doctor Helen Haines, to show you some support you’ve shown us through difficult times,” one reads from the eastern region of Victoria police.

Another, in child’s writing, says simply: “To Helen Haines, you’re very nice.”

australia.title: Helen Haines’s second leg amputated but she is stable and ‘a fighter’, husband says – as it happened
australia.snippet: Independent MP was struck by a car on Monday and her alleged attacker appeared in court on Wednesday ‘Deeply appalled’: politicians conde...
australia.content:
Helen Haines has had second leg amputated but is alive and stable

Phil Haines, the husband of Helen Haines, says the independent MP has now lost both of her legs after the alleged attack on Monday.

He said surgeons amputated her left leg on Monday and were hoping to save the right leg but could not.

The good news in all this is Helen is alive and she’s stable. That is the most important thing for our family. And I think when we reflect and talk about and think about Helen, the two most important parts of Helen for us as a family are her heart and her mind.

Her heart is huge. She is a very compassionate, caring, loving person. Incredibly supportive of all around her, her family, her community, anybody she comes across. And her mind. She has the sharpest intellect.

Phil Haines is providing an update to the media on behalf of the family. He says next month he and Helen are due to celebrate their 40th wedding anniversary.

What we learned today, 21 October

Thanks for joining us today. Helen Haines’s husband Phil and the governor general Sam Mostyn just spoke. Here’s what we learned.

  • Helen Haines has now lost both her legs following the alleged attack on Monday, her husband Phil Haines has told the media.

  • Phil Haines said anyone wishing to support the independent MP and her family should donate to the Save the Children Fund.

  • The governor general, Sam Mostyn, was invited by the family to speak alongside Haines.

  • Mostyn called for the public to remember kindness and civility, and to “disagree well”.

  • Mostyn said she has been keeping King Charles informed of the situation at the invitation of Haines’ family.

That’s where we’ll leave today’s coverage. Thanks again for joining us.

Mostyn and Phil Haines reiterate donating to Save the Children is the best way to support Helen Haines

Mostyn ends her address paying tribute again to Helen Haines and encourages everyone to donate to the Save the Children fund.

Phil Haines said Helen loves flowers, but donating to the fund is what she would want for those asking how they could support her.

Mostyn and Haines don’t take any questions. Mostyn says:

We’ve got to hope that that beautiful heart, that beautiful mind will be strengthened every day by our support and our commitment to be more like Helen as part of this great democracy.

It’s the very least we can do for someone who gave her life to others, represented her community and will go on and do so again with the kind of passion and care that we can all learn from, and that makes sure that we are a united country that can be so proud of everything that we stand for … I can’t wait to see her great heart and her great mind back in action exercising that great muscle of decency and teaching us how we can be better. Thank you.

‘Australians are yearning for kindness and care’: Mostyn

Mostyn, like the prime minister and others, speaks about the importance of robust democracy and being able to “disagree well” – in a bid to turn down the temperature across the country.

She says we should all do what Helen would at this time, which is reaching out to those distressed at this time and offer them care and comfort.

Remind ourselves, as Helen says all the time, that Australians have good hearts, great hearts and checking each of ourselves to ensure that we are in fact disagreeing well, not fighting with one another, not descending into violence and chaos and division. Most importantly that we learn or relearn to exercise our muscle of decency. And what I see and I saw with everything that Helen has done across Indi and well beyond is communities around Australia where Australians are yearning for kindness and care. And they’re asking us why we’ve lost the great skill of disagreeing well and with decency to each other.

She repeats Phil Haines’ words that the current situation is to take everything “day by day”.

She adds she has been keeping King Charles regularly updated on Haines’ condition at the invitation of Phil and their family.

‘Kindness, care and respect’: Mostyn pays tribute to Haines

Sam Mostyn says she’s “touched” she was invited by Phil Haines to speak with him, alongside his family.

She says she’s speaking to the public tonight as both the governor general, but also as a friend of Helen Haines.

She also thanks the first responders, hospital staff, community and barber Ricky who rushed out to help the member for Indi. Mostyn says she has spoken to Haines since Monday:

Now this violent attack on a much loved and respected sitting member of our federal parliament must be a moment for us to pause and to choose to be better.

In fact, it is bittersweet and quite difficult to talk about that. I was discussing this very topic with Helen just two weeks ago in Euroa, when we were both visiting a recovery hub dealing with the bushfire recovery, and we talked about the need for greater civility and engagement across our civic and public life.

As ever, Helen was actively thinking of ways in which the Australian community could come together and be encouraged to be both more engaged in our democracy, our great democracy and participate with the kind of engagement she has always done, kindness and care and respect.

‘Take things day by day’: Haines

Phil Haines is emotional as he ends his address to the media:

One thing I’ve learned in the last two days, reinforced by many people, is to take things day by day. I know it’s a cliche, but it’s a cliche for a very good reason. So I thank you all for being here. I thank you for listening. And please keep sending Helen your love and our family as well.

He then thanks the governor general, Sam Mostyn for travelling to Melbourne upon his request, and speaking to the media with him this evening.

He says he invited her at short notice and she came right away.

I invited her to come today at very short notice and she warmly and gladly straight away said yes. And it’s wonderful to have you here. Helen has the most incredible affection and respect for our governor general.

‘Helen’s road to recovery will be long and difficult but ... she is a fighter’: husband Phil Haines

Phil Haines pays tribute to all the first responders, police, paramedics and the community who have supported her since the alleged attack.

He asks for anyone who wants to support Haines, to donate to the Save the Children fund. He says Helen’s last official engagement on the day of the alleged attack was to speak at a legacy lecture for the charity.

He tells the media:

It’s amazing to think it’s only been two days since this horrendous accident or this horrendous incident took place.

Helen’s road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter. She is a determined person who will do her best with our support and love to recover. And that is what we hope for.

Helen Haines has had second leg amputated but is alive and stable

Phil Haines, the husband of Helen Haines, says the independent MP has now lost both of her legs after the alleged attack on Monday.

He said surgeons amputated her left leg on Monday and were hoping to save the right leg but could not.

The good news in all this is Helen is alive and she’s stable. That is the most important thing for our family. And I think when we reflect and talk about and think about Helen, the two most important parts of Helen for us as a family are her heart and her mind.

Her heart is huge. She is a very compassionate, caring, loving person. Incredibly supportive of all around her, her family, her community, anybody she comes across. And her mind. She has the sharpest intellect.

Phil Haines is providing an update to the media on behalf of the family. He says next month he and Helen are due to celebrate their 40th wedding anniversary.

Sam Mostyn and Phil Haines will be speaking shortly from Melbourne.

Here’s everything we know about her situation:

Helen Haines’s husband and governor general due to speak as MP remains in critical condition

Krishani Dhanji

Good evening, Krishani Dhanji here with you on the Guardian’s live blog.

The husband of Helen Haines, Phil Haines, and the governor general, Sam Mostyn, will be speaking to the media shortly to provide an update on the condition of the independent MP who was allegedly struck by a car on Monday and remains in hospital.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said earlier today Haines was still in a critical condition.

We’ll bring you that shortly.

What we learned so far

Thank you for joining us today. We are going to pause our coverage of the attack on Helen Haines for now. Here’s what has happened so far today:

  • The independent MP for Indi remains in a critical condition at the Alfred hospital in Melbourne. Haines has lost one leg, and surgeons operated on Tuesday in an effort to save the other.

  • Alleged attacker Brendan Nugent has been charged and appeared at a Wangaratta magistrates court this morning. The chief commissioner of Victoria police, Mike Bush, said police were considering further charges. Nugent has not requested bail and remains in custody.

  • Many in the Wangaratta community are still grappling with the events.

Wangaratta mayor says community is in ‘collective shock and sadness’

Caitlin Cassidy

The mayor of Wangaratta, Irene Grant, says the community is in “collective shock and sadness” after the alleged attack on Helen Haines.

Wangaratta council is holding a special meeting this afternoon to pass a resolution condemning violence against the independent MP, and maintaining “threats and intimidation have absolutely no place in our communities or our democracy”.

Grant told the meeting she was in “absolute disbelief that this should happen”:

This is a deeply distressing time for Helen, her family, her staff, and our entire community.

She said she had spoken to the governor general, Sam Mostyn, who expressed her support during what had been a “very difficult and emotional time”.

Grant said Mostyn had told her:

“Moments like this do not define us – what defines us is how we respond.”

The local state member, Tim McCurdy, is in attendance at the meeting, as our councillors and mayors from nearby regions.

Liberal MP says comments made in parliament last week were ‘regrettable’

The Liberal frontbencher Angie Bell has released a statement about the alleged attack on the independent MP Helen Haines.

Bell’s statement expresses regret about the comments she made last week, when she said the the small business minister, Anne Aly, and the prime minister should be “shamed and stoned in the square” over a decision made by the tax office. Aly condemned the comments as “racist” and “misogynistic”.

Bell said:

My thoughts are first and foremost with my friend Helen Haines and her family. This is a shocking attack on an outstanding MP who works diligently for her community.

She added:

My regrettable comment last week was a poor choice of words in the context of the challenges facing small businesses. It was not helpful or planned, which is why I immediately withdrew it and attempted to rectify this with Dr Aly.

While the motive for this horrific attack on Helen is not yet clear, there is absolutely no place for political violence in Australia. Australians must be free to disagree passionately, but there is no justification for threats or violence.

Helen Haines is the ‘MP we all wish we had’, David Pocock says

The independent ACT senator David Pocock says Helen Haines is “the MP we all wish we had”, telling the National Press Club in Canberra that working with her was one of “the great privileges of serving in our parliament”.

Pocock has also called out what he claimed was political actors using anger and hate “for political advantage”, including spreading misinformation.

“You [Haines] make our politics in this country better. That someone would deliberately hurt you, I find unfathomable,” Pocock told the Press Club in a speech.

He added:

We must meet this attack on you by doubling down on the values you represent, that you champion so hard in our parliament every day … now is the time to think about what brings us together. To defend our shared values, our democracy, and our freedom to live as Australians.

Pocock said he was concerned about increasing threats against politicians, an issue he spoke about with his wife, and the safety risks for people in public life.

Krishani Dhanji

Prime minister repeats calls to quell the anger in public discourse, citing protest at his office

Anthony Albanese has repeated calls to turn the political temperature down, telling News24 that his electoral office in Sydney has faced multiple protests.

He says the electorate office is largely for constituents to get help from staff with issues like Centrelink, migration, Medicare and healthcare.

He says he was forced to move offices, but protesters still demonstrate outside the old location.

He tells News24:

And the fact that tactics were used, such as regularly opening the door of my elector office, shoving in balloons full of what essentially were stink bombs, to make it uninhabitable for either staff or constituents, meant that it simply wasn’t tolerable, as well as the abuse that was suffered.

My old electorate office was in the grounds of the Anglican church St Clement’s there in Marrickville Road, and people going to church, it shared a car park as well. People going to church were being abused and it became such that the church ... wanted us to to move. So that has occurred. Bizarrely, the demonstration is still outside my former office.

Krishani Dhanji

Helen Haines remains in critical condition in Melbourne hospital, PM says

Anthony Albanese tells News24 he has spoken to Helen Haines’s husband this morning and that she remains in critical condition in hospital:

Helen remains in a critical condition ... It’s up to the family to make further statements when and and if they think that’s appropriate.

Krishani Dhanji

Parliamentarians are receiving briefings all day today from the Asio boss, the Department of Home Affairs and the Australian federal police, after the alleged attack on Helen Haines.

Anthony Albanese, who just attended a briefing for Labor MPs, said it was an opportunity for them to ask questions or raise concerns with the security bosses.

The crossbench and Coalition will get separate briefings today.

Albanese tells News24:

There’s been an increase in funding for security for members of parliament in the last couple of years, and this is an opportunity for people who feel anxious to be able to ask questions as well of the security agencies as well as the Department of Home Affairs.

Albanese is asked whether all parliamentarians could get individual security personnel. He says:

I think that risk assessments are made, and those risk assessments are done as best as possible. But here in this tragic circumstance with Helen Haines, she was getting something out of the boot of her car. Now people do need to go about their business.

australia.title: No bail for alleged Helen Haines attacker as police chief warns of Australia’s ‘febrile’ political environment
australia.snippet: AFP commissioner says MPs are generally concerned about growing volume of abuse and intimidation Follow our live blog for latest updates ...
australia.content:
The head of the Australian federal police has condemned a “febrile” political environment that has seen one person charged every week over the alleged threatening of MPs, as Victoria announces new steps to protect politicians.

But the AFP and Victoria police insist they had no intelligence to suggest 43-year-old Brendan Nugent would go on to allegedly drive a Toyota LandCruiser into the independent MP Helen Haines in a targeted attack.

Haines had one leg amputated after the alleged attack. Doctors had worked to save her second leg, but it was also amputated, her husband, Phil Haines, said at a press conference on Wednesday. Haines was in a stable condition, he said.

Nugent appeared at the Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday morning on charges of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and a federal offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official, along with cannabis possession.

In court, Nugent looked downcast in a grey jumper and stared straight ahead. The Tarrawingee man did not request bail, and will remain in custody until a committal mention on 4 February.

Magistrate Allison Vaughan noted Nugent had mental health and neurological concerns, and that this was his first time in custody. She asked for a mental health professional to see Nugent immediately after his court appearance.

His lawyer, Chirag Patel, said his client was not on any prescribed medication and was not withdrawing from any substances. Patel said Nugent was also suffering from concussion and idiopathic transverse myelitis – a rare inflammatory disorder of the spinal cord.

Further charges considered

At an earlier press conference in Melbourne, Victoria police’s chief commissioner, Mike Bush, said investigators were considering whether to lodge further charges against Nugent.

“That’s always a consideration,” Bush said. “Of course, we have to locate and follow the evidence, but this is a very serious and tragic incident, and we will be looking at all serious charges.”

Bush also said: “There was nothing known to us that would have arisen, or piqued our interest, or given any indication that [Nugent] was an immediate threat.”

At the same press conference, the AFP commissioner, Krissy Barrett, was asked whether her team was aware of Nugent’s social media posts, which included references to conspiracy theories and conflict in the Middle East.

“We didn’t have any specific intelligence that would have indicated something as atrocious as happened on Monday afternoon,” Barrett said.

“I can confirm we had no holdings or no intelligence to suggest that there was any threat to MP Haines.”

Bush said Victoria police had deployed more staff to Wangaratta to assure the local community, but said he was confident this was an isolated incident.

‘Growing volume of online abuse’

While Barrett and Bush did not allege a motive behind the alleged attack on Haines, which is still under investigation, they made general comments about the rising threat to MPs.

“The shocking alleged attack yesterday is what many had been dreading for some time,” Barrett said.

The AFP and Australia’s domestic intelligence agency, Asio, provided additional safety briefings to federal MPs on Wednesday. About six of these sessions have been held this year.

Barrett said federal MPs were increasingly worried about threats, and referenced a “growing volume of online abuse, threatening rhetoric, and intimidation, increasing political polarisation and anti-government sentiment”.

She continued to raise concerns about “conspiracy-driven and grievance-based behaviours, lone actors motivated by a convergence of personal grievance, mental health vulnerabilities, and ideological concerns, and the potential for violence to emerge with little or no forewarning – particularly where individuals have no previous protection intelligence footprint”.

Bush highlighted similar concerns and said Victoria police would create a centralised process to help monitor threats against MPs.

“We want a single-stop shop to report these things and have the ability to be very proactive,” Bush said.

On Tuesday, the Victorian Animal Justice party MP Georgie Purcell said she had received more security support as the partner of the federal MP, Josh Burns, than she did in her own role.

She urged Victoria police to create a dedicated unit, similar to that which exists within the AFP for politicians or people in high-profile roles.

“They have teams that can monitor fixated people, shifts in language, in behaviour, see if they’re escalating, and then work out whether the continued behaviour could constitute an event,” Purcell said.

Bush, who was due to address state MPs and ministers on Wednesday afternoon, said there were no resourcing restraints that would prevent Victorian politicians from receiving the protection they felt they deserved.

world.title: Nigeria confirms Ebola case as outbreak spreads into western Africa
world.snippet: Case in Africa’s most populous country was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its c...
world.content:
Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the health ministry said.

The woman began showing symptoms on 7 October and was admitted to a hospital in Abuja four days later, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola. It is unclear when she arrived in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country.

The health minister, Muhammad Pate, said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. “We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had,” he said.

Uganda’s ministry of health said the patient had only transited through Uganda and that she is a Nigerian woman who had been on a business trip to Congo’s eastern region. The Nigerian authorities have not disclosed her nationality.

“Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement. The ministry insisted Uganda has “no confirmed active Ebola cases”.

Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the outbreak spreads across the region. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has since recorded nine infections. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases, but it later declared itself free of the virus.

Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control, said on X that “we are facing an extremely serious threat,” with a fatality rate of nearly 50% of cases.

“This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa,” he said.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control said two weeks ago it was stepping up surveillance following the detection of Ebola in Kenya and strengthening the country’s preparedness for a potential outbreak.

“These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of health care workers,” the agency said.

Nigeria established an Ebola taskforce in June after the outbreak in Congo in mid-May.

The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has infected more than 9,500 people and killed more than 4,600 people.

The latest Ebola outbreak is the fastest-spreading on record and is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, the 11,000 people killed in West Africa’s regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, WHO has said.

world.title: RFK Jr’s ‘deities of vaccine research’ raided by police in Guinea-Bissau
world.snippet: Police seize doses of hepatitis B vaccine from people at center of dispute over research on African newborns Controversial vaccine resear...
world.content:
Controversial vaccine researchers who have been praised by Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) secretary, had their offices in Guinea-Bissau raided by judicial police, who seized doses of hepatitis B vaccines, officials said on Facebook.

The researchers have been at the heart of an ongoing dispute over research on African newborns, supported by $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and matched by the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation for a total of $3.2m.

The police search took place on Monday, involving “investigative procedures aimed at clarifying the circumstances related to the said batch of vaccines”, according to the social media post, which was translated from Portuguese. The announcement noted that seizing the immunizations did not point to “irregularities in the quality, safety, or effectiveness of the vaccines”.

The Bandim Health Project recently posted a letter of approval for the trial from Guinea-Bissau’s national ethics committee at the ministry of public health, dated 14 July and signed by the committee’s president, Mouhammed Djicó Ould Ahmed. A Danish research ethics committee, which had to change its rules to consider a clinical trial, also approved the study earlier this month.

Quinhin Nantote, the health minister of Guinea-Bissau’s transitional government, disputed reports that the trial would move forward.

“This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese on Thursday.

The study was redesigned over the summer, but it would still deny hepatitis B vaccines to 7,000 newborns in the first six weeks of life, in a country where about one in five adults have the virus. Hepatitis B kills 15% to 25% of people with chronic infections, causing cancer and liver failure, and newborns are particularly vulnerable – but vaccination within 24 hours of birth is safe and highly effective at preventing illness.

Any study that would deny the vaccine to participants was “unethical and exposes newborns to serious and potentially irreversible harm”, said Tarik Jašarević, a spokesperson for the World Health Organization (WHO), calling hepatitis B vaccination at birth an “essential public health intervention”.

Through its country office in Guinea-Bissau, the WHO and its partners have been advising the ministry of health on the planned introduction of the hepatitis B vaccine and the potential impact of this study, Jašarević added.

The Bandim Health Project was founded by anthropologist Peter Aaby in 1978, and it is now co-led by his wife, Christine Stabell Benn, an epidemiologist.

Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, calling them “the deities of vaccine research” at a recent anti-vaccine conference. He has several times referenced the results of a study they conducted on the diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (DTP), which the same researchers later conducted again and found completely different results. Even so, Kennedy called Aaby a “very famous” researcher on Joe Rogan’s podcast in 2023 and cited his research when he halted US funding to Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance.

Stabell Benn was a member of the hepatitis B working group of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), helping present evidence to the US committee that voted to end the universal birth recommendation before such decisions on vaccines were stayed by a federal judge. Stabell Benn also hosted a podcast with Tracy Beth Høeg, a former top official with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) who said she wanted to end “unnecessary” vaccines.

Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, the lead researcher on the project, did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about the trial and the police search.

The Bandim organization is deeply enmeshed in Guinea-Bissau but has done little to improve the country’s health and research capacities in five decades of operation, according to a report from the non-profit Stand Up for Science (SUFS). The organization is now fundraising to help roll out the vaccines at birth to all newborns in the country.

“Our investigator encountered significant distrust of Bandim by the citizenry of Guinea-Bissau,” said Colette Delawalla, an American health researcher and founder of SUFS. “However, because of the lack of public health infrastructure, Bandim is often the only option in situations where people are desperate to access medical care of any kind.”

The police raid underlines the fact that Guinea-Bissau is a “fragile” nation that experienced a military coup less than a year ago, Delawalla said. The country lacks the stability needed for clinical trials, she added.

“Guinea-Bissau is in the difficult situation of trying to protect their youth, their future, from exploitation by two powerful western nations and they are using what leverage they have to do so,” Delawalla said.

world.title: US grants deportation reprieve to migrants from Ukraine and Sudan
world.snippet: DHS says migrants ‘retain protections’ after temporary protected status was set to expire on Monday Send us your questions about immigrat...
world.content:
More than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in what amounts to a temporary reprieve after their right to stay in the country was set to expire on Monday.

Temporary protected status was set to end on Monday for about 101,000 Ukrainians and 1,800 Sudanese. But the DHS said an announcement “will be made at the appropriate time”. Until then, the department said in a written statement, Ukrainians and Sudanese in the US covered by those temporary measures “retain protection”. The department did not indicate how long they could stay or when a final announcement would be made on their status.

The DHS did not respond to a question about whether they can keep their work permits, but TPS generally allows people to work while their protections remain in effect.

The decision marks another incident where the Trump administration, which has previously sought to end these temporary protections from deportation and send people back to their home countries, has allowed people covered by the temporary status to stay in the country but without giving any guidance as to how long.

Yuriy Boyechko, CEO of Hope For Ukraine, a non-profit that provides humanitarian aid in Ukraine and helps resettle newcomers in the US, described the government’s announcement as “last-minute patches”.

It is a “bandage that has been placed on a wound that does not solve the real issue,” he said. “It’s time for US to come up with some normal path to permanent residency for all these people,” Boyechko noted. He emphasized that they cannot safely return to Ukraine.

Andrew Arthur, a national-security and immigration expert at the Center for Immigration Studies, a Washington thinktank that favors lower immigration, said the government will eventually decide but faces no deadline. Until then, nothing changes, he said.

“It’s simply going to be an extension until it is a termination,” he said. “It’s beyond cavil that both Sudan and Ukraine are experiencing ongoing armed conflict, and therefore the secretary is well within his authority to continue TPS for each of them.”

The Trump administration has already terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria.

But in a change in practice roughly a month ago, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorians whose TPS was set to expire on 9 September. In that case they also said that they were going to make a decision at the appropriate time and that in the meantime, people from El Salvador could continue to work and live in the US.

Activists and a bipartisan group of lawmakers have been raising the alarm over the upcoming deadline for TPS to expire for Ukrainians, arguing that conditions remain unsafe for them to return home amid the war with Russia.

Ukraine was first designated for TPS in April 2022, following Russia’s full-scale invasion two months earlier. The Biden administration subsequently extended the designation, most recently in January 2025, when the DHS authorized an additional 18 months of protection through October 2026.

The TPS program for Sudan was established in 1997, and since then, successive US administrations have extended it due to the armed conflict and political instability that have plagued the African nation.

Monday’s decision comes two weeks before the midterm elections, when Trump’s hard line immigration policies will face a test at the ballot box.

world.title: Kenyan starvation cult leader guilty of murder of 190 children and one adult
world.snippet: Paul Mackenzie and his church set up sect that ordered followers to starve themselves and their children, say prosecutors A Kenyan court ...
world.content:
A Kenyan court has found the starvation cult leader Paul Mackenzie and about 30 others guilty of murder over the deaths of ⁠190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult-related disasters in recent history.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast ⁠in south-eastern Kenya.

Prosecutors say Mackenzie and ⁠his Good News International Church organised ​a Christian doomsday sect in which they ordered followers to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.

Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve but the ⁠court rejected that argument.

In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered from the Shakahola forest. Many were severely decomposed, and only 26 of them were able to be identified.

Monday’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into the other deaths are continuing.

Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.

Mackenzie was in ​court, wearing a striped polo shirt and red trousers, sitting alongside his wife, ‌one of the co-accused.

He was silent, ‌staring into space before the ruling was handed down.

Relatives of some of those who died in the forest gathered to hear the judgment at Mombasa high ‌court.

Francis Wanje, 62, lost eight family members including two grandchildren to the cult.

Speaking before the verdict, he said: “It has been really a heavy thing [for] us as a family, and it has really taken us very far in terms of psychological problems … I was hoping for this particular day.”

The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the coastal forest more than three years ago.

It raised questions over how Mackenzie was able to continue to operate despite having been on the radar of the authorities since 2017 when his premises were searched by police. In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.

The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.

Kenya’s president, William Ruto, said in 2023 that government agencies should have been ​able to prevent the deaths. He said he took responsibility as president.

People with direct knowledge of the cult’s activities said Mackenzie planned the mass starvation in three phases: first children, then women and young men, and finally the remaining men.

Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic, some of his followers told Reuters for a 2023 article.

Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene ⁠sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.

The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in mid-March 2023, when a local man told ​police that his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives say he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police ​arrested him again in April 2023 and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.

Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths including terrorism-related ones, which he has denied.

Prosecutors say while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles (30km) from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

world.title: Drone attack near market kills 80 in Sudan
world.snippet: Witness says drone struck twice at transport hub in al-Dibab, in one of deadliest single attacks of war A drone strike near a market in s...
world.content:
A drone strike near a market in southern Sudan on Sunday evening killed 80 people, mostly commuters catching rides home.

Ahmed Wadi, a witness, said the attack in the town of al-Dibab in West Kordofan state left “50 bodies who I helped bury, one of them my own brother Mohamed”.

Using a satellite internet connection to circumvent a communications blackout, Wadi also said 47 other people were transported to the nearest town, al-Mujlad. A medical source, requesting anonymity for his safety, said 30 of them died from their injuries.

The medic said: “A total of 80 people were killed in the drone strike on al-Dibab, and another drone strike on al-Mujlad injured four who are currently being treated.”

Wadi said the drone struck twice, 10 minutes apart, “on a transport hub where people gather to travel back to their villages after the market day ends”.

The attack is one of the deadliest single strikes since war broke out in April 2023 when a power struggle between the Sudanese armed forces (SAF), headed by Gen Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, erupted into violence in the capital, Khartoum.

The RSF-declared administration, known as Tasis, accused the army of carrying out Sunday’s strike. All of West Kordofan state is under RSF control.

Sudan has witnessed an escalation in the use of drones in the war. Between January and April, drone strikes accounted for at least 880 civilian deaths, more than 80% of all conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan.

After drone strikes on a busy livestock market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur state, on Friday, the SAF said they had killed RSF fighters, but the RSF accused the military of killing 30 civilians.

The fighting in Sudan has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced many more. It has been fuelled by foreign powers with vested interests who are supporting sides in the conflict.

Last week, Rosemary DiCarlo, the undersecretary-general for political and peacebuilding affairs at the UN, warned the security council that the conflict and humanitarian crisis was deteriorating “with no breakthrough on the horizon”.

She said: “They [the warring parties] are not moving closer to dialogue. On the contrary, they seem to believe that they can make greater gains on the battlefield and that continued external support will allow them to pursue their objectives by force.”

AFP contributed to this report
